requirements.text: The contractor must develop the curriculum for and administer the AI Prep program for Track A (AI Prep 4 Internships) and/or Track B (AI Prep 4 Jobs).
requirements.quote: OSWD seeks to award contracts to up to two (2) qualified program administrators to develop the curriculum for and to administer AI Prep for Track A and/or Track B.

requirements.text: Track A (AI Prep 4 Internships) must provide low-income matriculating undergraduate students with AI training aimed at securing paid internship opportunities at leading tech companies.
requirements.quote: Track A: AI Prep 4 Internships will provide low-income matriculating undergraduate students with AI training with the goal of securing paid internship opportunities at leading tech companies.

requirements.text: Track B (AI Prep 4 Jobs) must connect low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment to AI jobs through an accelerated training or bootcamp that serves as an alternative to traditional degree programs.
requirements.quote: Track B: AI Prep 4 Jobs will connect low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment with AI jobs through an accelerated training or bootcamp that serves as an alternative to traditional degree programs.

requirements.text: The program must serve New Yorkers who are currently underrepresented in the tech industry and who cannot reasonably access training on their own.
requirements.quote: AI Prep will have two dedicated tracks to serve New Yorkers who are currently underrepresented in the tech industry and who cannot reasonably access training on their own.

ambiguities.description: The text does not define eligibility criteria for 'low-income' participants (e.g., an income threshold or benefit-program proxy), which determines recruitment scope and enrollment targets a bidder must price and staff.

It is unclear whether a bidder may propose for both tracks under a single contract or must submit separate proposals per track, and whether the 'up to two (2)' awards means one administrator per track.

The text does not define what counts as "low-income" for student eligibility, nor how many students must be served or how many internship placements must be secured; a bidder would ask for the eligibility threshold and the required cohort/placement scale to size the program and price it.

The text does not specify the stipend amount, duration, or whether internship wages are paid by the administrator or the host employer; a bidder would ask who funds stipends and internship pay and at what rate.

The text does not specify the stipend amount, duration, or how much of the $2M per-track cap must be allocated to stipends versus training delivery, which materially changes the budget model; the bidder would ask what stipend level and share of the award are expected.

The program must be 'immersive' and deliverable part-time or full-time, but neither the total training hours nor the minimum/maximum program duration per participant is defined; the bidder would ask what intensity and length constitute an acceptable immersive schedule.

The text sets a 250-participant minimum as a "should" while giving priority to applicants serving more than 400, leaving unclear whether 250 is a pass/fail threshold or merely a scored preference. The bidder would ask how participant counts are scored and whether a proposal below 250 is disqualified.

"The majority of graduates" and "closely related field" are undefined, and no measurement period or verification method is given, so the bidder cannot tell what outcome commitment it is making. The bidder would ask what percentage and time frame define success and how employment outcomes are documented.

The low-income threshold is marked with a footnote reference that is not included in this text, so the definition of "low-income" is unknown. The bidder would ask which income definition or eligibility standard applies.

The RFP does not say how experience in a domain is demonstrated or measured (e.g., years of experience, number of students served, contract values), so a bidder cannot tell whether its track record qualifies or what evidence to submit.

The text refers to "one track" and "both tracks" without defining what the tracks are or how many exist, which determines whether the $2M or $4M cap applies; the bidder would ask how many tracks the program has and what each covers.

ESD may deny reimbursement of expenses it deems ineligible, but the text does not state which expense categories are eligible; the bidder would ask for the eligible cost categories or a cost manual governing reimbursement.

The budget must be "mapped to the program duration," but the program duration is not stated in this text; the bidder would ask what the grant period length is and whether the budget must be broken out by month, quarter or year.
The participant stipend level is a required budget line but no cap, per-participant amount or eligible use is given here; the bidder would ask what stipend range or ceiling applies.

The text says there is no cost-match requirement but that cost-matching earns additional points, without stating how much match is needed or how points scale. A bidder would ask what match percentage or amount maximizes scoring and whether any minimum is expected.

The chunk refers to "Proposed definition" without stating what definition is being proposed or what criteria an alternative must meet. A bidder would ask which definition this refers to and what justification standard applies.

The exact list of data points is left to ESD and will only be fixed during contract negotiation, so the bidder cannot know the full reporting scope or effort to price; the bidder would ask for the definitive data-point list and reporting frequency/format.

The text does not define how 'low-income' is determined (e.g., income threshold or program eligibility criterion), which affects data collection design; the bidder would ask for the definition to apply.

The Corporation reserves the right to change any of the dates, so the bidder cannot rely on the stated schedule; the bidder would ask whether the submission deadline and contract start date are firm or subject to change and how changes will be communicated.
The anticipated debriefing timeframe is listed as TBD, leaving the post-award schedule open; the bidder would ask when debriefings will occur.

The college-student and other-participant items ask for cost per student/participant and placement rates but do not define the reporting period or whether figures are per cohort or cumulative, so a bidder cannot tell which numbers to report.

The phrase "if not already addressed" leaves it unclear whether the employer-coordination and New York items may be omitted when covered elsewhere in the proposal, or must be cross-referenced explicitly.

The text requires a monthly timeline running through completion of internships or full-time jobs by the first cohort but gives no cohort start date or program period, so the bidder cannot anchor the schedule; the bidder would ask for the intended program start date and the required end date for the first cohort.

The proposal must state a proposed stipend level and/or other supports, but the text does not say whether a stipend is required, what it must cover, or whether it is subject to a cap; the bidder would ask whether stipends are mandatory and whether any funding ceiling applies.

The text does not define "low-income participants" (e.g., which income threshold or eligibility standard applies), which determines the denominator for the completion-rate metric and thus the commitment the bidder makes; the bidder would ask which definition or standard to use.

It is unclear whether the placement rate is measured at graduation, within a set period after graduation, or over a defined tracking window, and whether paid internships must meet a minimum duration; the bidder would ask for the measurement period and definition of placement.

The bracketed note says a uniform schedule of all fee components should be established "in case of complex cost structure" but does not define what counts as complex or what the schedule must look like; the bidder would ask whether a prescribed cost schedule template exists and when it is required.

The Technical Proposal must include a "Cost of Services" section, yet pricing is normally submitted separately; bidders would ask whether cost information belongs in the technical volume or a separate price proposal, and whether including it risks disclosure.

The "Diversity Practices Questionnaire" is listed as required content but is not provided in this text; bidders would ask where the questionnaire form is obtained and whether it is a separate document.

The text says failure to submit any listed requirement "may result in the rejection" of the proposal, leaving it unclear whether any omission is disqualifying or curable; a bidder would ask whether missing items can be supplied after submission and whether the order of items is strictly enforced.

The chunk states that late proposals will not be considered but gives no submission deadline or time zone; the bidder would ask for the exact due date and time and whether the Dropbox upload timestamp governs receipt.
The folder naming convention requires the "date of Submission" but does not specify a date format (the example uses MM.DD.YYYY); the bidder would ask which format is required.

The text says OSC approval "may be required" for contracts over one million dollars paid with State monies or awarded non-competitively, so it is unclear whether this procurement will actually be subject to OSC review and how long that approval could delay contract execution; a bidder would ask whether OSC approval applies here and what schedule impact to assume.

The contract requires performance "in a timely and professional manner" and assessment via progress reports and periodic meetings, but no reporting frequency, format or meeting cadence is defined here; a bidder would ask how often progress reports and meetings are expected so it can staff and price the effort.

"Applicable professional standards" is not defined, and the no-charge correction obligation is limited to errors in "the progression of its work"; a bidder would ask which standards apply and how long the correction obligation lasts after delivery.

The clause allows the Corporation to accept a claim asserted after the 30-day window if it decides the facts justify it, so it is unclear whether the 30-day deadline is a hard bar or waivable; a bidder would ask how strictly the deadline is enforced.

client_situation.text: The RFP is issued by Empire State Development (ESD), a New York State economic development corporation whose mission is to promote a growing state economy, encourage business investment and job creation, and support diverse local economies through loans, grants, tax credits, real estate development and marketing.

ESD's Office of Strategic Workforce Development (OSWD) was created as part of a $350 million workforce development investment announced by Governor Kathy Hochul in April 2022, and is charged with aligning workforce programs to employer needs and creating opportunities for unemployed, underemployed and underrepresented workers.

ESD has identified Artificial Intelligence as one of the state's highest-growth sectors, pointing to Cornell Tech research, companies using AI for analytics and automation, and state-backed initiatives such as Empire AI.

ESD's stated pain point is that rapid AI advancement risks widening economic inequality, because many well-paying AI jobs require specialized education and technical training that lower-income New Yorkers cannot access.
ESD also cites tech recruiting practices that favor students at elite schools and those with personal connections to prominent technology companies as a barrier AI Prep is meant to level.

The procurement is subject to a Procurement Lobbying Law restricted period running until contract approval, during which bidders may contact only the designated contacts (Julia Borukhov, primary; Jordan Kaplan, secondary) by email at AI.Prep@esd.ny.gov.

goal.text: ESD seeks to award contracts to up to two qualified program administrators to develop the curriculum for and administer the AI Prep applied training program, covering Track A and/or Track B.

Track A, "AI Prep 4 Internships," requires the administrator to deliver a comprehensive AI technology training program for low-income matriculating undergraduates, including paid internship placements at leading New York tech companies leading ultimately to full-time jobs.

Track B, "AI Prep 4 Jobs," requires an accelerated training or bootcamp alternative to degree programs that equips low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment with in-demand AI technical and professional skills and connects them to full-time AI jobs.

Both tracks must include targeted outreach and recruitment, an application and assessment process, industry-informed online AI curriculum, participant stipends and wrap-around supports such as mentors or success coaches, and employer relationship-building to generate placements.

The selected administrator(s) will operate the program over an initial term of up to 18 months, with possible renewal or extension based on performance, need and availability of funds, and an anticipated contract start date of January 1, 2026.

Awarded administrators must track and report data including applicant, enrollment and completion counts with low-income percentages, paid internship and full-time job placement rates, and participating colleges and employer partners, with the exact list set during contract negotiation.

success_criteria.text: Proposals are scored out of a maximum of 100 points by an ESD selection committee, allocated as Firm Qualifications 15, Experience 25, Project Plan 30, Cost of Services 20 and Diversity Practices 10.
The program must serve a minimum of 250 participants, with priority for applicants proposing to serve more than 400 participants, and over 50% of participants must be low-income.
The majority of program graduates must secure paid internships or full-time employment in artificial intelligence or a closely related field.

The Project Plan must include a monthly timeline through first-cohort placement, proposed training duration, cohort size, stipend level, and estimated annual performance against three metrics: total participants served, percentage of low-income participants completing the curriculum, and placement rate.
The Project Plan must be supported by 1-page resumes of key personnel and letters from partner employers committing to provide paid internships or full-time employment to graduates.
Questions are due by August 29, 2025, ESD answers are due September 12, 2025, and proposals must be submitted by 2:00 PM ET on October 1, 2025, with award announced November 14, 2025.

Proposals must be uploaded as a main folder named "company name – RFP title – date of Submission" containing separate Administrative and Technical Proposal subfolders to the Dropbox at https://www.dropbox.com/request/AIPrep; fax, hardcopy and email submissions are not accepted and late proposals will not be considered.

constraints.text: ESD will invest up to $2M per track (up to $4M total), and budgets exceeding $2M for one track or $4M for both tracks over the total contract period will not be considered.

Indirect costs are not an allowable cost under this grant, and the budget must be mapped to the program duration across Staff Salary and Benefits, Wraparound Supports and Participant Stipends, and other program costs such as curriculum development, marketing and events.
There is no cost-match requirement, but applicants can earn additional scoring points for cost matching, which must be indicated in the budget template.

Applicants must be non-profit or for-profit entities with experience in at least three of four domains: academic services to college students, high-tech accelerated training programs, serving low-income populations, and working in the New York market.
The resulting contract carries a 30% MWBE participation goal and a 6% SDVOB participation goal, with MWBE and SDVOB Utilization Plans (OCSD-4) required and good faith efforts documented.

The selected contractor must carry Commercial General Liability of $1M per occurrence and $2M aggregate, Sexual Abuse and Molestation insurance of $1M, statutory Workers' Compensation and Disability coverage, and name ESD as additional insured with a waiver of subrogation.

Appendix A (ESD IT Security Standard Brief) and Appendix B (Diversity Practices Questionnaire) are referenced by the RFP but their content is not included in the RFP text, so bidders must obtain them separately.

Contractor staff are subject to ESD approval, staff continuity is expected through project completion, and no subcontracting is permitted unless indicated in the proposal and approved in writing by the State Project Manager.

solution.summary: ESD is buying program administration, not software: the bidder delivers a full-service AI Prep operating capability — outreach, assessment, industry-informed online curriculum, stipends and wrap-around supports, employer placement, and outcome reporting — configured around ESD's two tracks and priced within the $2M-per-track cap. The solution is built in four phases: a 60-day mobilisation after the anticipated 1 January 2026 start (curriculum finalisation, employer commitments, systems and compliance set-up), a launch cohort recruited and assessed against a defined low-income standard, delivery of immersive part-time or full-time online training with mentors and career coaches, and placement plus outcome tracking through the 18-month initial term. The bidder proposes as a single lead entity (with named subcontractors disclosed in the proposal) and offers Track A, Track B, or both, with a separate costed budget for each track so ESD can award one or two administrators. Delivery is by a named core team of program director, curriculum lead, employer partnerships lead, success coaches and a data/compliance analyst, all subject to ESD approval and continuity expectations. A dedicated compliance workstream runs alongside delivery to carry the MWBE/SDVOB, insurance, lobbying-law, vendor-responsibility and reporting obligations that the contract imposes, and it also owns the bid-side calendar that gets the bidder's questions to ESD by the August 29, 2025 deadline.

components.title: Program design, curriculum and credential architecture
components.description: Delivers the industry-informed online AI curriculum for Track A and Track B, built with an employer advisory group that reviews technical skills and learning milestones each cohort. The curriculum is structured as an immersive schedule that can run part-time or full-time, with defined skill-attainment assessments at each milestone and a stated credential (or explicit statement that none is issued) on completion. Curriculum development is completed or finalised in the mobilisation phase and refreshed each cohort against employer input, and the design documents the monthly timeline through first-cohort placement, training duration, cohort size and stipend level.

claims.text: ESD intends to award contracts to up to two program administrators covering Track A and/or Track B, so the curriculum is designed as two separately costed track variants.
The anticipated contract start date is January 1, 2026, which sets the mobilisation window before the first cohort.

components.title: Outreach, recruitment and application/assessment process
components.description: Runs a targeted recruitment campaign for New Yorkers underrepresented in tech who cannot reasonably access training on their own, with channel plans for CUNY/SUNY campuses, community-based organisations and workforce partners. Delivers an online application and evaluation process with a documented low-income eligibility determination, a needs assessment that records each participant's barriers to success, and an individual success plan that routes supports accordingly. Recruitment targets are set to meet or exceed the 250-participant floor with a stretch plan above 400, and to keep low-income enrolment above 50%.

claims.text: The program must serve a minimum of 250 participants with priority for proposals above 400, and over 50% of participants must be low-income.

components.title: Training delivery, stipends and wrap-around supports
components.description: Delivers and manages the cohort-based training itself: instruction, cohort management, attendance and progress tracking, and professional development support throughout training. Each participant receives a stated stipend at the proposed level plus wrap-around supports — a mentor and a career coach with industry expertise, plus barrier-specific supports identified in the needs assessment. Delivery is staffed for both part-time and full-time schedules so participants with employment or caregiving obligations can complete the program.

claims.text: Both tracks must include participant stipends and wrap-around supports such as mentors or success coaches.

components.title: Employer partnerships and placement engine
components.description: Cultivates and maintains relationships with leading New York tech employers to inform curriculum content and generate paid internship and full-time AI openings, supported by employer commitment letters submitted with the proposal. Runs a placement function that matches participants to paid internships (Track A) and full-time AI roles (Track B), prepares them for interviews, and tracks placements through to hire. Placement support is designed to meet the commitment that the majority of graduates secure paid internships or full-time employment in AI or a closely related field.

components.title: Performance data, reporting and ESD access
components.description: Implements a participant data system that captures every required data point — applicant, enrolment and completion counts with low-income percentages, paid internship and full-time placement rates with low-income percentages, participating colleges and employer partners — and makes the data available to ESD on request. Produces the progress reports and periodic meeting cadence that support ESD's performance assessment, and reports against the three annual performance metrics (participants served, low-income completion rate, placement rate) estimated in the proposal. The data model is built to absorb the additional data points ESD fixes during contract negotiation without re-platforming.

Budget lines cover staff salary and benefits, wraparound supports and the participant stipend level, and other program costs including curriculum development, marketing and events. Indirect costs are excluded entirely, and any cost match the bidder offers is indicated in the budget template to earn the additional scoring points.

components.description: Runs a mobilisation phase from the anticipated 1 January 2026 start to first-cohort launch, covering curriculum finalisation, employer commitment conversion, systems set-up, compliance filings and staff onboarding for ESD approval. Provides day-to-day program management with a named core team, monthly timeline tracking through first-cohort placement, and a staff continuity plan that notifies ESD immediately of any proposed change and offers the substitute's experience and an interview before approval. assumptions.text: Low-income eligibility is assumed to be defined by Pell Grant eligibility for Track A students and by an income threshold tied to state/federal benefit-program eligibility for Track B participants, with the definition stated in the proposal and applied consistently across recruitment, stipends and reporting.
The bidder is assumed to be able to propose for both tracks under a single response with separately costed track budgets, and the two awards are assumed to be one administrator per track.

Stipends are assumed to be paid by the administrator from the $2M per-track award, with internship wages paid by the host employer, and the stipend level is assumed to be set by the bidder within the track cap rather than by an ESD-prescribed rate.

An immersive schedule is assumed to mean a full-time cohort of roughly 12 weeks or a part-time cohort of roughly 24 weeks, with the specific hours and duration proposed by the bidder as the training duration required in the Project Plan.
The 250-participant figure is treated as a scored floor rather than a disqualifier, so the proposal commits to a participant count above 400 to capture the stated priority.

Placement success is assumed to be measured as paid internships or full-time AI-related roles secured within six months of program completion, verified by employer confirmation or pay documentation, and the proposal commits to a placement rate above 50%.
The budget is assumed to be presented by month across the 18-month initial term, with the option of a renewal period priced separately, since the RFP does not fix the breakout granularity.

The reporting data-point list is assumed to be the set named in the RFP plus a small negotiated margin, and the data system is scoped to that superset so contract-negotiation additions do not change the price.

The 30% MWBE and 6% SDVOB goals are assumed to apply to total contract value and to be met through demonstrated good faith efforts with a waiver route if certified firms are unavailable, rather than as pass/fail thresholds.
OSC review under Public Authorities Law §2879-a is assumed to apply given the contract value, so the mobilisation plan absorbs a possible approval delay before the January 1, 2026 start.
Progress reporting is assumed to be monthly written reports plus quarterly review meetings, since the RFP sets no cadence, and the effort is priced on that basis.

Appendix A (ESD IT Security Standard Brief) and Appendix B (Diversity Practices Questionnaire) are assumed to be obtainable from ESD before submission and to impose no requirements beyond standard state data-handling and diversity-practice disclosure, so the participant data system is designed to state-government security baselines.

Cost information is assumed to belong in a separate Cost of Services volume referenced from the Technical Proposal, resolving the tension between the required Technical Proposal section and the prohibition on extra content.

Schedule A concerns are assumed to be submitted as a separate written letter accompanying the Administrative Proposal rather than inside the proposal narrative, satisfying both the concerns requirement and the prohibition on including Schedule A documentation.

risks.title: Schedule A terms unseen but binding, and its concerns must be filed blind
risks.description: Schedule A sets the standard contract terms the successful respondent must accept, yet its text is not in the RFP. The bidder must decide whether to accept unknown terms and file written concerns with its Administrative Proposal, while the RFP simultaneously forbids including Schedule A information in the submission. If Schedule A contains unacceptable liability, indemnity or data-ownership terms, the bidder either walks away after award or absorbs unplanned legal and insurance cost.
risks.justification: Schedule A is referenced as a mandatory contract term (R115, R260) but is absent from the RFP, and R258/R259 pull in opposite directions on how concerns are filed, so the bidder cannot price or accept the terms knowingly.
risks.mitigation: Request Schedule A through the designated contacts before the August 29, 2025 question deadline, and state in the proposal that acceptance is conditional on review of Schedule A; file concerns as a separate letter accompanying the Administrative Proposal, as the proposed solution assumes.

risks.title: MWBE 30% and SDVOB 6% goals carry liquidated damages and payment withholding
risks.description: The contract sets a 30% MWBE and 6% SDVOB participation goal, with good faith effort documentation, quarterly Workforce Utilization Reports and monthly SDVOB compliance reporting. Failure to meet the goals can trigger liquidated damages equal to the shortfall and withholding of payment, and the RFP does not settle whether the goals apply to total contract value or subcontracting spend or whether good faith efforts alone suffice.
risks.justification: The damages and withholding provisions are explicit (R191, R195, R196, R250), but the base against which the goals are measured and the waiver standard are left open, so exposure depends on facts the RFP does not settle.
risks.mitigation: Identify certified MWBE and SDVOB subcontractors before submission and build them into the Utilization Plans and the budget; ask ESD to confirm the measurement base and the waiver route, and price a compliance analyst to run the reporting cadence.

risks.title: Stipend level and its share of the $2M per-track cap are undefined
risks.description: The RFP requires a stipend line in the budget and a stated stipend level in the Project Plan but gives no rate, duration or expected share of the award. If ESD expects a stipend near a full-time wage for 250+ participants, the stipend alone could consume most of the $2M per track, leaving too little for instruction, coaching and placement — and the bidder only learns this after award.
risks.justification: Stipends are mandatory (R016, R051, R084) and the cap is fixed (R034), but the RFP leaves the rate and allocation open, so the budget model turns on an unsettled fact.
risks.mitigation: Ask ESD before the deadline what stipend range and share of the award it expects; state the proposed stipend level and the participant count it supports as an explicit assumption in the proposal, and show the cost model at that level.

risks.title: Placement commitment above 50% rests on employer letters the bidder must secure
risks.description: The RFP requires the majority of graduates to secure paid internships or full-time AI roles and requires employer commitment letters with the proposal, but does not define the measurement window or verification method. The proposed solution commits to a placement rate above 50% measured within six months, an assumption the bidder is making on ESD's behalf; if employers do not convert letters into hires, the bidder carries the performance risk.
risks.justification: Placement is a core scored outcome (R041, R098) and the proposed solution's six-month measurement window is an inference, not an RFP term, so the commitment could exceed what the bidder can control.
risks.mitigation: Secure signed employer commitment letters with named role counts before submission, and state in the proposal the placement definition, measurement window and verification method the bidder will report against.

risks.title: Appendix A IT security standard unknown, so the data platform may be under-scoped
risks.description: Appendix A, the ESD IT Security Standard Brief, is referenced but not included, so the security controls the participant data system must meet are unknown. If it imposes state-standard controls such as hosting in approved environments, encryption, access logging or third-party assessment, the proposed data system and its cost will need rework after award.
risks.justification: The proposed solution explicitly assumes Appendix A imposes nothing beyond standard state data-handling baselines, an assumption the RFP does not support because the document is missing.
risks.mitigation: Obtain Appendix A before submission and price the data system to its actual controls; if it is not released, state in the proposal that the security architecture and price assume standard NYS data-handling baselines and that any additional controls will be handled as a change order.

risks.title: Appendix B Diversity Practices Questionnaire missing while worth 10 scoring points
risks.description: The Diversity Practices Questionnaire is required in the Technical Proposal and is scored at 10 of 100 points, but the form is not in the RFP. A bidder that cannot obtain it either submits an incomplete Technical Proposal or loses the full diversity score, which can decide a competitive award.
risks.justification: The form is both a mandatory submission item (R102, R113) and a scored section, and it is absent from the RFP, so the loss is near-certain unless ESD releases it.
risks.mitigation: Request Appendix B from AI.Prep@esd.ny.gov before the question deadline and prepare the diversity narrative in advance so the questionnaire can be completed quickly once released.

risks.title: Administrative forms and OCSD/MWBE/SDVOB templates not supplied
risks.description: A long list of required submission items — Non-Collusive Bidding Certification, Conflict of Interest Attestation, 139-j/139-k forms, Vendor Responsibility Questionnaire, Iran Divestment statement, EO 16 and EO 177 certifications, OCSD-1/2/4, ST-220-CA, W-9 and the NYS Businesses form — are provided only as external links or not at all. Missing or mis-ordered items may render the proposal non-responsive, and the bidder must assemble and verify all of them in the weeks before the October 1, 2025 deadline.
risks.justification: The RFP says omission may result in rejection and requires items in a set order, and several forms (OCSD-1, OCSD-2, OCSD-4, MWBE and SDVOB Utilization Plans) are not included, so the risk turns on how strictly ESD enforces completeness.
risks.mitigation: Build a submission checklist mapped to the RFP's listed order, download every linked form at kickoff, and ask ESD in writing whether omissions can be cured after submission.

risks.title: Participant floor of 250 versus the 400+ priority is not a settled threshold
risks.description: The RFP sets a 250-participant minimum as a 'should' while giving priority to proposals above 400, and the proposed solution commits to more than 400 to capture the priority. If 250 is in fact pass/fail and 400 is only a scoring preference, the bidder has priced a larger program than needed; if the commitment is contractual, under-recruiting against 400 becomes a performance failure.
risks.justification: The proposed solution treats 250 as a scored floor and commits above 400, a design choice that raises cost and delivery risk if the RFP's intent differs.
risks.mitigation: Ask ESD how participant counts are scored and whether a proposal below 250 is disqualified; state the committed participant number and the recruitment assumptions behind it in the proposal so the commitment is bounded.

risks.title: Low-income definition is undefined and drives eligibility, stipends and reporting
risks.description: The RFP does not define 'low-income' — the footnote reference is missing — yet the definition determines recruitment scope, the 50% low-income enrolment target, stipend eligibility and the completion and placement denominators. The proposed solution assumes Pell eligibility for Track A and a benefit-program income threshold for Track B; if ESD applies a different standard, recruitment and reporting must be rebuilt.
risks.justification: The definition is required for multiple mandatory data points (R058–R062) and the 50% target (R040), and the proposed solution's definition is an explicit inference.
risks.mitigation: Ask ESD to confirm the low-income definition and whether an alternative may be proposed under R055; state the definition and its documentation method in the proposal so the enrolment and reporting commitments are tied to it.

risks.title: Immersive schedule length and intensity are undefined, so staffing and stipend cost float
risks.description: The RFP requires an immersive program deliverable part-time or full-time but sets no hours or duration. The proposed solution assumes roughly 12 weeks full-time or 24 weeks part-time; a longer or more intensive schedule required by ESD would raise instruction, coaching and stipend costs against a fixed $2M cap.
risks.justification: Training duration must be stated in the Project Plan (R082) and drives the budget, but the RFP leaves the definition of 'immersive' open (R027).
risks.mitigation: State the proposed hours and duration per track in the Project Plan as the bidder's definition of immersive, and ask ESD whether a minimum intensity applies.

risks.title: OSC approval and a 1 January 2026 start leave a thin mobilisation window
risks.description: Award is announced November 14, 2025 and the contract is anticipated to start January 1, 2026, but the contract is not enforceable until the Office of the State Comptroller grants any required approval. If OSC review runs past January, the 60-day mobilisation compresses and the first cohort, curriculum finalisation and compliance filings slip, while the 18-month term may still be measured from the original start.
risks.justification: The RFP does not confirm whether OSC review applies here or how long it takes, and the proposed solution only assumes the mobilisation plan absorbs a possible delay.
risks.mitigation: Ask ESD whether OSC approval applies and whether the 18-month term runs from execution or from January 1, 2026; state in the proposal that mobilisation begins on contract execution and that the first-cohort date shifts with any approval delay.

risks.title: Technical Proposal content limits conflict with the required Cost of Services section
risks.description: The RFP requires a Cost of Services section inside the Technical Proposal while also forbidding any information beyond what is specifically requested, and the proposed solution resolves this by placing cost detail in a separate volume referenced from the Technical Proposal. If ESD reads the prohibition strictly, the cross-reference or the separate volume could be treated as non-conforming or the price could be judged incomplete.
risks.justification: R103 and R114 pull in opposite directions and R112 mandates a Cost of Services section, so the resolution depends on how ESD interprets its own instructions.
risks.mitigation: Ask ESD in writing whether cost information belongs in the Technical Proposal or a separate price volume; follow the answer exactly and keep the Technical Proposal to the listed sections with bookmarks matching them.
